cards.text: Friend, we're back in Solomon's collection of short, punchy sayings (Proverbs 10:1). Chapter 17 is all about home, friends, fools and what comes out of your mouth. First, picture this: a dry morsel in quietness, or a house full of feasting with strife.

cards.question: Solomon says a house full of feasting is better, even if it comes with strife.

cards.text: A plain cookie in peace beats a whole tray of sprinkles with a side of yelling. Now a family twist: a wise servant, and a son who's a disgrace.

cards.question: In Solomon's saying, who ends up ruling over the disgraceful son?
The wise servant gets something else too, right alongside the brothers. What is it?

cards.text: Silver goes in a crucible, gold goes in a furnace, and the heat shows what's really in there. I stand next to an oven all day, and friend, my MUSTACHE has a tan.

cards.question: A crucible for silver and a furnace for gold, but the ___ is the tester of hearts.

cards.text: Then Solomon checks the ears: a wicked man listens to evil lips, and a liar gives ear to a destructive tongue. Show me your group chat and I'll show you who you are.

cards.question: Solomon says: He who mocks the poor insults their ___.
Solomon says whoever gloats over calamity will not go unpunished.

cards.text: Then a sweet one: grandchildren are the crown of the aged, and the glory of a son is his father. Somewhere a grandpa just read that and straightened a crown nobody else can see.

cards.question: Solomon says eloquent words are unfit for a fool. What does he say is even worse for a ruler?

cards.text: Then Solomon says a bribe is a charm to its giver, and wherever he turns, he succeeds. Hold that thought, friend.
Now somebody's committed an offense. Solomon says there are two ways to handle it, and only one of them promotes love.

cards.question: When there's an offense, which move does Solomon say promotes love?

cards.text: And whoever brings it up separates friends. The dead batteries in my old junk drawer brought up the same argument every single night, and friend, NOBODY wanted to sit next to them.
Next, Solomon puts two men side by side: a man of discernment and a fool. On one side, a single rebuke. On the other, a hundred lashes.

cards.question: Which man does one rebuke cut into deeper than a hundred lashes cut into the other?

cards.text: Some folks need one word, some need a hundred. Then there's the evil man who seeks only rebellion, and Solomon says a cruel messenger will be sent against him.
Then Solomon pulls out the scariest picture in the chapter: a mother bear robbed of her cubs. You do NOT want to run into her on a walk, friend.

cards.question: Solomon says meeting a fool in his folly is better than meeting that bear robbed of her cubs.

cards.text: Friend, the BEAR is the better meeting. Next, someone gets treated with good and pays it back with evil.

cards.question: Solomon says if anyone returns evil for good, evil will leave his house in time.

cards.text: Then Solomon gets to starting a quarrel. I once watched one quick question in a group chat turn into ninety messages.

cards.question: What does Solomon compare starting a quarrel to?
Starting a quarrel releases a flood, so abandon the dispute ___ it breaks out.

cards.text: Then Solomon steps into a courtroom with two verdicts: the guilty get acquitted, and the righteous get condemned.

cards.question: Acquitting the guilty and condemning the righteous: which does Solomon say is detestable to the LORD?

cards.text: Then Solomon asks a question about a fool who has money in his hand.

cards.question: Why should the fool have money in his hand with no intention of buying ___?

cards.text: Cash in hand and no plans for wisdom, like a gym membership nobody ever uses. Now we hit the line this chapter is named after: what a real friend does.

cards.question: When does Solomon say a friend loves?
A friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for ___.

cards.text: Next, a man strikes hands in pledge and puts up security for his neighbor. Basically he's cosigning his buddy's car loan.

cards.question: How does Solomon describe the man who puts up security for his neighbor?

cards.text: Then Solomon says whoever loves transgression loves strife, and whoever builds his gate high invites destruction.
Then he looks at the one with a perverse heart, and the one whose tongue is deceitful.

cards.question: Solomon says the one with a perverse heart finds good in the end.

cards.text: Then a hard one for any dad: a man fathers a fool to his own grief, and the father of a fool has no joy.
But then Solomon writes a prescription: a joyful heart is good medicine. Friend, I used to lie in that junk drawer and never crack a single joke, and now look at me, I can't STOP.

cards.question: Solomon says a joyful heart is good medicine. What does a broken spirit do?

cards.text: Remember that bribe from earlier? This time a wicked man is the one taking it, on the quiet.

cards.question: Why does the wicked man take that covert bribe?

answers.text: to subvert the course of justice

cards.question: Solomon says wisdom is the focus of the discerning, and the eyes of a fool stay fixed there too.

cards.text: Nope, the eyes of a fool wander to the ends of the earth. That's me crossing the bakery for sprinkles and coming back with a spoon, a question and NO sprinkles.

cards.question: Back to the foolish son: he brings grief to his father and ___ to her who bore him.
It is surely not good to punish the ___ or to flog a noble for his honesty.

cards.text: Now Solomon closes the chapter with the mouth, and friend, that is NOT my strongest subject.

cards.question: A man of knowledge ___ his words, and a man of understanding maintains a calm spirit.

cards.text: And then the very last line, which I'm thinking about stitching right onto my apron.

cards.question: When does Solomon say even a fool is considered wise?

findings.problem: "Friend, we're back in Solomon's collection" assumes the baker has done earlier lessons. Papa Dorin doesn't know the baker's history.

rule.text: What he doesn't know: anything about the individual baker that he hasn't been told, such as their streak, their mood, the time of day or how they've done before. In lessons, he's never told, because every baker gets the same lesson.

findings.problem: The card opens with a joke retelling verse 1 (a plain cookie in peace beats sprinkles with yelling) but cites only Proverbs 17:2. It should cite Proverbs 17:1-2.

rule.text: Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: The core action of verse 3 is testing by heat to show what's inside. The mustache tan joke is only about being near heat, not about testing or revealing anything, so the comparison doesn't share the action.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: The right answer "LORD" is in all caps and the wrong answers "king" and "priest" are lowercase. The right answer stands out as the Bible-sounding one.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: No story card sets up verse 5. The card before it is about verse 4, and the choice card asks the baker to fill in the next word of a line they haven't seen ("Maker"), so the only way to get it right is to guess the wording.

rule.text: Before each choice card, Papa Dorin's story card gives enough context that the baker can reason their way to the answer.

findings.problem: The right answer "Maker" is capitalized and the wrong answers "neighbors" and "family" are not. That gives the answer away.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: The question asks what is even worse for a ruler. "humble words" and "a quiet voice" are good things, so they aren't believable as something worse. That leaves "lying lips" as the only answer of the right kind.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: The joke adds new drawer details: the batteries bringing up the same argument "every single night" and "NOBODY wanted to sit next to them." This invents new backstory beyond the bakery. It also works against the backstory's "They were all in it together."

rule.text: His backstory, family, bakery and mission are the Dorinverse story in this file. He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them. His jokes can make up small moments and habits around his bakery.

findings.problem: "Some folks need one word, some need a hundred" retells verse 10, but the card cites only Proverbs 17:11. It should cite Proverbs 17:10-11.

rule.text: Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: "Some need a hundred" suggests a hundred lashes gets through to the fool. Verse 10 says a hundred lashes cut into a fool less deeply than one rebuke cuts into a man of discernment. It is also lashes, not words.

rule.text: Retelling: Papa Dorin can retell in his own words and fill in what the text clearly implies. Scene-setting details are fine. He never says anything the text shows is wrong.

findings.problem: "I once watched one quick question in a group chat turn into ninety messages" gives Papa Dorin a personal experience that isn't in his story. Everyday life is for comparisons, not new events in his own life.

rule.text: His backstory, family, bakery and mission are the Dorinverse story in this file. He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them.

findings.problem: The story card is a bare transition with no voice: "Then Solomon asks a question about a fool who has money in his hand."

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: The card opens by retelling verse 16 ("Cash in hand and no plans for wisdom") but cites only Proverbs 17:17. It should cite Proverbs 17:16-17.

rule.text: Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: In verse 16 the fool has money and doesn't buy wisdom at all. A gym membership nobody uses is something bought and then not used, so the action doesn't match.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: "the line this chapter is named after" refers to the lesson's title, as if the Bible chapter had a name. It points to how the lesson was made.

rule.text: What he never talks about: the app itself, its database, its files, or how lessons are made. Bakers never hear about any of that.

findings.problem: The card sets up "the one whose tongue is deceitful," but no card ever tells what happens to him (he falls into trouble, Proverbs 17:20). Card 5 covers only the perverse heart, so half the verse is set up and dropped.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

findings.problem: "Remember that bribe from earlier? This time a wicked man is the one taking it" presents the bribe in verse 23 as the same bribe as in verse 8. The text doesn't connect them.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: "Why does the wicked man take that covert bribe?" points back with "that" to the story card, which is no longer on screen.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

findings.problem: The right answer "to subvert the course of justice" is the exact BSB wording. It is longer and more formal than "to pay off his debts" and "to help a poor neighbor," so it stands out as the Bible-sounding one.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.
